At the same time, at Elea in southern Italy, Parmenides argued the opposite in a poem: being is, non-being is not; what is can neither be born, nor perish, nor change. The motion we see belongs to deceptive opinion.

Achilles, the fastest of runners, will never catch the tortoise that started ahead: he must first reach the point it just left, then the next, forever. Mathematicians would take more than two thousand years to explain that an infinite sum of durations can be finite.

Empedocles of Akragas, in Sicily, proposed four roots, earth, water, air and fire, mixed by Love and separated by Strife. Xenophanes, for his part, noted that if oxen could draw, they would make ox-headed gods.

Colours and tastes are mere conventions of our senses. All these thinkers are called "pre-Socratics", a word coined in the late 18th century; their writings are lost and survive only as fragments, collected by Hermann Diels in 1903.

He rose to Minister of Crime, then spent years on the road offering his ideas to other princes, without being heeded. Back home at about 68, he taught: tradition credits him with 3,000 pupils.

A prince raised in luxury, he left it to become a wandering ascetic, almost to the point of starving himself. Neither luxury nor deprivation brought him liberation. At Bodh Gaya, sitting under a fig tree, he attained awakening: he became the Buddha, "the awakened one".

At about 17, he entered Plato's Academy, where he stayed nearly twenty years. Around 343 BC, Philip II of Macedon hired him as tutor to his son, the future Alexander. In 335, he returned to Athens and taught at the Lyceum, where discussions were held walking under the covered walkway, the peripatos.

Épicure, né à Samos en 341 av. J.-C., ou: Epicurus, born on Samos in 341 BC, opened his school in Athens around 306, in a garden he owned: it would be called the Garden. He welcomed many women there, a rare thing, and lived simply among friends. Friendship, for him, was worth more than power or wealth.
Le but est l'ataraxie, l'absence de trou: The goal is ataraxia, freedom from disturbance of the soul, and aponia, freedom from bodily pain. His followers summed up his teaching as a four-part cure: don't fear the gods, don't worry about death, the good is easy to get, the bad easy to bear. "Death is nothing to us": when it is here, we are no longer. Of some three hundred treatises, only maxims, three letters and charred fragments from Herculaneum remain.

To Alexander the Great, who offered him whatever he wanted, he replied that he should stand out of his sun.

Cynics, Epicureans, Stoics and Sceptics all sought, after Alexander, a wisdom to live by.

Hobbes (1651) : la sécurité contre la li: Hobbes (1651): security in exchange for liberty. Locke: protecting natural rights. Rousseau (1762): the general will.
En 1748, dans De l'esprit des lois, Mont: In 1748, in The Spirit of the Laws, Montesquieu wrote: "To prevent the abuse of power, things must be so arranged that power checks power." Hence the separation of the legislature, which makes laws, from the executive, which applies them, and the judiciary, which judges. He did not start from nothing: he drew on Locke and on what he observed in England.
Even in a democracy the danger remains. Tocqueville, in Democracy in America, feared the tyranny of the majority, which can oppress as surely as a king, and more discreetly. John Stuart Mill replied in 1859 with On Liberty: the only legitimate reason to limit someone's liberty is to prevent harm to others. Over himself, the individual is sovereign.

En 1971, dans Théorie de la justice, Joh: In 1971, in A Theory of Justice, John Rawls proposed an experiment: choose a society's rules behind a veil of ignorance, without knowing what place you will have in it. You might be born poor, ill or in a minority. Rawls thought you would then choose equal liberties for all, and accept inequalities only if they also benefit the worst off.
D'autres pensent l'État par la force ou: Others think of the State in terms of force or resistance. For Max Weber, in 1919, the State is what successfully claims the monopoly of legitimate physical violence. Henry David Thoreau, jailed for a night in 1846 for refusing to pay tax, theorised civil disobedience, which Gandhi and Martin Luther King would read. And Karl Popper, in 1945, stated the paradox of tolerance: unlimited tolerance towards the intolerant ends up destroying tolerance.

Pour Descartes, l'esprit, res cogitans,: For Descartes the mind, res cogitans, and the body, res extensa, are two different substances. It remains to explain how they communicate. He proposed the pineal gland, chosen because it is single at the centre of the brain rather than paired. We now know that it mainly secretes melatonin, the sleep hormone.
En 1949, dans La Notion d'esprit, Gilber: In 1949, in The Concept of Mind, Gilbert Ryle mocked this dualism: he called it the "ghost in the machine", a philosopher's myth. For materialism, the mind is what the brain does. For functionalism, it is defined by what it does, not by what it is made of: a well-organised machine could then have a mind. Alyca follows the debate with interest.

En 1950, dans Computing Machinery and In: In 1950, in Computing Machinery and Intelligence, Alan Turing replaced the question "can a machine think?" with a game: the imitation game. A judge converses in writing with a human and a machine; if they cannot tell them apart, by what right deny the machine the word "think"?
En 1980, John Searle répond avec la cham: In 1980 John Searle replied with the Chinese room. A man shut in a room receives questions in Chinese and, using a rule book, sends back perfect answers without understanding a word. Manipulating symbols according to rules would therefore not be enough to understand. Passing the Turing test would not prove consciousness. Alyca finds the example a little personal.

En 1974, Thomas Nagel demande : quel eff: In 1974 Thomas Nagel asked: what is it like to be a bat? You can know everything about echolocation without knowing what it is like to live it. These subjective feelings, the red of your red, are called qualia. In 1982 Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a scientist who knows everything about colour but has lived in a black and white room: the day she sees a tomato, does she learn something?
En 1995, David Chalmers sépare les probl: In 1995 David Chalmers separated the "easy" problems of consciousness, explaining attention or perception, from the "hard problem": why is all this accompanied by feeling? And in 1983 Benjamin Libet measured brain activity, the readiness potential, that precedes the felt decision to move by about a third of a second. Its interpretation regarding free will remains hotly debated.

Une dinde est nourrie chaque matin à 9 h: A turkey is fed every morning at 9 o'clock. Day after day it concludes that it always will be. It has its throat cut on Christmas Eve. This is the popular version of an example by Bertrand Russell, who spoke of a chicken, in 1912 in The Problems of Philosophy. It illustrates Hume's problem of induction: no accumulation of observations logically guarantees the next one.
Dans les années 1920 et 1930, le cercle: In the 1920s and 1930s the Vienna Circle, with Carnap, Schlick and Neurath, wanted a science based on experience and judged metaphysics meaningless, neither true nor false. Popper countered with falsifiability. And Norwood Russell Hanson pointed out in 1958 that observation is not neutral: do Tycho Brahe and Kepler, watching the sunrise, see the same thing?
Induction : des milliers d'observations: Induction: thousands of observations do not prove the next one (Hume, Russell's chicken). Observation depends on what you know.
La thèse de Duhem-Quine dit qu'on ne tes: The Duhem-Quine thesis says you never test a hypothesis alone, but together with a whole web of auxiliary hypotheses: if the experiment fails, the fault may lie with the hypothesis, the instrument or a side theory. Which to sacrifice? In 1846 Uranus was not following its predicted orbit. Rather than throw out Newton's mechanics, Le Verrier assumed an unknown planet. Johann Galle found it less than a degree from the predicted position: Neptune.
Le Verrier recommence pour expliquer les: Le Verrier tried again to explain Mercury's anomalies and predicted Vulcan. It did not exist: general relativity was needed. Imre Lakatos drew a rule from this: a research programme is "progressive" when it predicts unexpected things that turn out true, and "degenerates" when it only patches up its failures after the fact.
Duhem-Quine : on teste un réseau, pas un: Duhem-Quine: you test a web, not a lone hypothesis. Neptune (1846): a successful rescue. Vulcan: the theory had to change.
En 2015, l'Open Science Collaboration te: In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration tried to reproduce 100 psychology studies published in good journals. It found a significant result for only about 36 % of them. That is not necessarily fraud: often an effect too weak, a sample too small, or analyses chosen after seeing the data. The replication crisis has pushed researchers to preregister studies.
La relecture a ses failles. En 1996, le: Peer review has its flaws. In 1996 the physicist Alan Sokal got the journal Social Text to publish a hoax arguing that quantum gravity is a social construct; no physicist had reviewed it. Paul Feyerabend provoked in 1975 with Against Method: no rule was respected by all the great discoverers. Scientific realism replies with Putnam's no-miracles argument: if our theories were not roughly true, their success would be a miracle.
